utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mucibabic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The examination by Mr. Visnjic will continue in a moment. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration which you made at the beginning of your evidence to tell the truth continues to apply to your evidence today. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mucibabic.

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yesterday in your evidence you told us that the evening briefings were recorded in a notebook and that it was mostly you and Colonel Paskas who actually took the minutes. I would now like to go through an Exhibit with you, that's 3D1094.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is the so-called briefing book, and I would like to go through the pages in that book for the purposes of authentication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this also not yet translated into English?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document has been translated in such a way that individual days are translated as separate documents. 90 per cent of this document, and in particular for the relevant period until the 9th of July, that has been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there any reason why for today's purposes we need to see the English versions?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's just -- it's just -- I want the witness to identify some things in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, on your arrival in The Hague you inspected this document in detail?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to go through with you -- through some dates with you and I would like you to assist me if you can to identify some persons that wrote this document. This is the first page of this document. Could you please tell me what is the date when this page was written and could you please identify who wrote that.

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This page was done on the 24th of March, 1999, in the time between the -- between 7.15 and 7.45, that was the morning briefing. This is not my handwriting, and I can't recognise the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please move to page 5 of this document, that's in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, what do we see in front of us?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the briefing at 1900 hours on the 24th of March, 1999, and this is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now go to page 6 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What do we see in front of us, General?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the briefing at 2400 hours, that's the night of the 24th until -- to the 25th of March, 1999, and I don't recognise the handwriting, it's not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please move to page 7 on e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the briefing at 2100 hours, the 25th of March, 1999, and this is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the second part, the second part, that's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we scroll down a little bit, a little bit lower. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you now tell us what this is?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We see in front of us a very short briefing that was at 2200 hours, the 25th of March, it ended the 2340, again this is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now move to page 11, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, what do we see in front of us?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the briefing on the 26th of March, 1999, it began at 800 hours and ended at 900 hours, and this is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 12, please. Could we move it a little bit up, please, in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the briefing of the 26th of March. It started at 2030. This is not my handwriting. I can't recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move to page 17 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the briefing of the 28th of March. This is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 23 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the briefing of the 29th of March that started at 2030. This is not my handwriting, I can't recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now move to page 24, 25.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not my handwriting either.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now move to page 31 in e-court. Could we scroll it down a little bit, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The signature below this handwriting that I was unable to recognise indicates that the minutes were taken by Colonel Milivoj Gutovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me whether you can recognise the briefing of the 30th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is not my handwriting and I can't recognise it. I can only identify the person by the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please now move to page 43 in e-court and page 42 before this one, please, so that we can see whether we have a signature for the previous date. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, do you recognise this signature?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the signature of Colonel Golic who was the deputy of Paskas.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now could we move to page 43, that is the briefing of the 31st of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, do you recognise this handwriting?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not my handwriting and I can't recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at page 47 in e-court, that's the 1st of April, 1999. Do you recognise the handwriting here?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not mine and I can't recognise it unless I see the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, could we please look at page 46 to see who signed the briefing of the 31st of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the signature of Colonel Bozo Maljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was Bozidar Maljkovic?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Maljkovic was the desk officer in the first department with Colonel Paskas.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now please look at page 52, please, in e-court. The date is the 2nd of April.

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see page 53 here in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please move to the previous page in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the briefing of the 2nd of April. Again, this is not my handwriting and I can't recognise it. I can only recognise it if I see the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Fine. Let us look at page 56 then, or rather, if we can look at page 55 first.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you can scroll down to the very bottom, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Whose handwriting is this on page 55?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's rather illegible, but this is Dragan Paskas's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move on to page 56 now, this is the 3rd of April now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You told us already that you can't recognise the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But could we then look at page 65 in e-court, and before that, page 64, so that we can see if we have the signature for the date that is the 3rd of April, 1999. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, whose signature is this?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the signature of Colonel Zlatomir Sibulovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Who was Colonel Sibulovic at that time?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Sibulovic was the desk officer in the operations department.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at page 60, or rather, 70. This is the 5th of May [as interpreted] 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, do you recognise the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my handwriting. I think that this is Dragan Paskas's handwriting, but it would be a good idea to look at the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Fine. Let me just correct the transcript, it should read the 5th of April.

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 5th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at page 51, or rather, I apologise, page 69 -- no, no, that was the previous handwriting. I'm sorry. Page 74. [In English] That's my mistake. [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: That's the last page for the minutes of the 5th of April, 1999, General, could you please look at the signature.

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minutes were signed by Colonel Dragan Paskas.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now move to the next page, that's page 75.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the handwriting here?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not my handwriting and I can't recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at page 77.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no signature on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at the 7th of April, 1999 -- actually, it's page 78 in the e-court. Whose handwriting is this?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, let's not go further. You had the opportunity of looking at this document in detail before testifying here. Can you please tell us what you established globally for the period after the 7th of April, 1999. Which persons wrote the logs from that period until the end of the war in the briefing book?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, attorney Visnjic, after that date all the briefing books were signed either by me or by Colonel Dragan Paskas.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we looked at this document and I already spoke with the Prosecution about this. We established that certain pages were missing in this document and those are pages 5, 17, 18, 71, 77, 80, 118, 163, and 279. I spoke with the Prosecutor. I think most of the pages other than one copy actually should just be blank pages followed by the text, but the Prosecutor will discuss this in more detail with the witness. This is the copy that we received when we requested it and this is the copy that we are presenting now to the Court as an exhibit. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Any Defence counsel with cross-examination? No. Mr. Mucibabic, you'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General. You mentioned yesterday at the very beginning of your evidence that you graduated from the academy in 1970; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in part of your answer you mentioned that that was a generation that had several witnesses here. I take it those would have been colleagues of yours from that time and friends; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my colleagues from the same class, same generation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you name some of those persons from your class who have been witnesses here?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. Immediately before me, this was Colonel Stanisa Ivkovic; and then before him I saw on the link that Colonel Novkovic also testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Anyone else you can remember right now?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the moment. I can't remember anyone else. The only thing is that among the accused, General Pavkovic is also from our class.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you -- before you came to testify in this trial, did you have occasion to discuss that fact that you were going to testify or to discuss with Mr. Ivkovic or Colonel Novkovic about their having testified here?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see them for a year for sure, and I saw attorney Visnjic once a year ago and then here now on Tuesday. So I didn't think about this before coming here to the Tribunal and I didn't have any contacts with anyone about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you mentioned these daily briefings in the evening during the war where you took notes for several of the sessions. Between the 24th of March and the date in June when the war ended, were there evening briefings every single day as far as you recall?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, they -- there were evening briefings every evening, a total of 90 briefings were held, these evening briefings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if there is -- there's a gap in the notebook where there are no notes for a particular day, what would that mean to you?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the handwriting -- or actually the manuscript of the briefing book was copied entirely. I saw the blanks from the lawyer where it says that the conclusions that we glued in and that were typed were removed for technical reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry, I don't think I heard about that before. So are you saying that at the end of each day certain conclusions from the briefings were typed up and then physically pasted into the notebook for each day? Is that what you just said?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the briefing and in -- pursuant to orders of the chief of the Supreme Command and the chief of the cabinet and the person who took the minutes, we would usually meet; and from the notes we would together formulate the conclusions which were then much clearer to see and were better formulated. And then we would paste them in, in order to be more precise and for those who would subsequently read them to have an easier job of it was just a compilation of what two note-takers recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm a little unclear about that. So after the meeting you said that we would meet and from the notes we would together formulate the conclusions which were then much clearer to see and were better formulated, and then we would paste them in. Who met after the meeting? For example, let's say this is a meeting where you were taking the notes, after the meeting who did you meet with to do that?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of the meeting, the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, General Ojdanic, would issue assignments which were quite clear, but when writing we couldn't note everything down. The chef de cabinet would sit next to me or next to Colonel Paskas, and he would also note down these conclusions. Then after the meeting we would go through it, look at it in detail, because this was a summary of the entire daily work and the briefing which the chief would then read.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And it appears from our copy then of this notebook that those typewritten summaries have either been removed or else they were covered over when this copy was made; would you agree with me about that?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the assumption. I would rather not comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were there typewritten conclusions after every one of the meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the second half, yes; in the first half, I think not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I ask because the page numbers given as missing pages only amount to nine. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but you will see that for some of the pages we have there's writing on the top third or the top fourth, and then the bottom half is blank white.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've already seen that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I'm trying to find one where you were the note-taker on a date after the 6th of -- or the 7th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we go to e-court page -- I think it would be page 119.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I can see that I'll be able to tell you in a minute, General, if this is the page I wanted to ask you about. Do you recognise the handwriting on that page?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would this be Colonel Paskas's handwriting?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it is, but in order to be sure in my answer I would need to look at the signature, but I think it is, also the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go back one page to get the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This appears to be the 18th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then if we could go forward to page 121, I believe, we'll get the last page of this date, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You'll see what I was talking about with the -- you'll see that -- there's no signature on this page and I'm wondering if this is perhaps one of the pages where typewritten summaries have been pasted in and then when this copy was made, that it had either been removed or it was covered over when this page was copied. But we have no signature on this date.

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but these conclusions you can see. This is 11 -- you can see when they were written.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Are you saying that in this case it appears the conclusions were written out rather than typed?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know because I was not taking the notes that day, so I don't know what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you see the number in the upper left-hand corner here, the handwritten 126?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you were reviewing this document before coming to court, did you notice the handwriting numbers on I think all the pages in the document? Did you have a chance to notice anything about them?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noticed that there was some numbers, but I didn't go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know when or how or who put those numbers on there?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you were taking notes during the war, you didn't number the pages, did you?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The book was logged in and it was probably paginated, and I assume that the pagination here was something that happened later during copying or during some other procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Or perhaps during archiving?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps, I don't know. On the 22nd of June I handed over the documents and later I didn't see them again anymore until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you haven't seen the original since 1999 when you turned it in, correct?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I took up another duty after that and I devoted myself to an entirely different job.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this is page number 126 which is our e-court page number 121. This is from a meeting on the 18th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to the next number in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The next page of this document we have, Colonel, is a page number 130. You'll see in the upper left-hand corner if we can go to the top half of this page.

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this is for a briefing on the 21st of April, so we go from the 18th to the 21st and we go from page 1 -- we go from page 126 to 130. So it appears we're missing three pages: 127, 128, and 129, and two meetings for the 19th of April and the 20th of April, because you told us that you met every evening during war. Do you know what happened there?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On my screen it's the 23rd of April, page 138.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Now do you see page 130?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is 130, the 21st of April, and this is indeed my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I will tell you that in the copy of the document I have we do go from page 126 to page 130 and there don't appear to be any minutes or notes for meetings on the 19th of April or the 20th of April. Do you know why that would be?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there then. I came on shift on the 21st of April. We spent a total of 90 days at the command post. For a full 50 days, I was there and this was kept throughout those 50 days. I think the briefing took place also on the remaining 40 days and this must be some sort of error in your documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, there's certainly enough errors in my documents, but this is not my document. This is a document from the VJ. But you're certain that there were meetings every evening and that I think you told us after April 7th notes were taken of every meeting, correct?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was the shift leader, I can say that they were, yes. The order and the work-plan by the Supreme Command Staff was such that there should be a briefing every day pursuant to the rules, and I should assume that briefings took place on those days as well. But I can't say with any degree of certainty simply because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to e-court page 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you told us, Colonel -- or, General, you don't recognise this handwriting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I have on the screen right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my handwriting; I do recognise that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I did say so before, didn't I?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I must have got my note wrong. Now, General, this was on the - I can't tell the date. Is this on the 28th of March?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If it's page 17 in e-court it's the 28th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We are missing pages 17 and 18 -- or we're missing pages numbered 17 and 18 from the document which appears to have been for the date of the 27th of March. Do you recall whether or not there was a meeting on the 27th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 27th of March, yes. Yes, there was a meeting. I was at the command post at the time, some work was done, and a briefing took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, did you take the notes on the 27th?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so, and I think I actually saw those notes in some document or other.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But they don't appear to be in here. Do you know what would have happened to the notes for the 27th of March?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what could have happened, but I noticed with the lawyer, too, that there were notes that weren't identical. Copying errors must have been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The notebook that you used to take notes in, I see on the copies here it appears that there are holes in the middle of the page. Is that how the original notebook looked? Did it have holes punched so it could be put into a binder, for example? You see the small hole on the left side of this page.

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see the hole. I think this hole is used to tie these sheets together and for stamping eventually, just to make sure no sheet came loose.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you were taking notes, how did -- how was the notebook kept between meetings? If you took the notes on this day, on the 28th of March, where did the notebook remain until the next evening meeting, did you keep it with you or did you pass it on to somebody else who was going to be keeping the notes or was it kept in a particular safe location between meetings? How was that preserved?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document was preserved in keeping with the rules governing work at the command post in the operations department. It was sealed in a box.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where was that box, in whose office?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This box or safe deposit box was in the operations department room.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we look at e-court page 75.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, if I'm correct, this should be for a meeting on the 6th of April. This is numbered page 78 in the upper left. Do you recognise that handwriting?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that this handwriting most probably belongs to Colonel Paskas, but for the sake of history one has to look at the signature, although I don't think he actually signed it. But this is Colonel Paskas's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I would agree with you, it does look similar to other ones sign by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page, this is e-court page 77 and it's numbered page 79 in the upper right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you'll see at the very bottom of the page --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go back one page -- or I guess could we put these two pages side by side, page 76 and 77 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Bear with me, General, I'm trying to get page 76 on the left-hand side of the screen and 77 on the right. These are -- in the document that we have a copy of, these are consecutive and you'll see page number 79 on the left and on the right it's page number 81. It appears we are missing page number 80, but because I can't read Serbian would you read the last three lines on what's numbered 79 and then look at the top of the next page and tell me if it appears that something's missing.

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is obvious here is that a page is missing. On page 79 I see something illegible and pale. I think this was Lieutenant-General Grahovac contributing, and then you see tasks starting with number 3. Obviously during the interval there had been some sort of discussion and then the final contribution by General Ojdanic and then the tasks, 1, 2, followed by 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I also note that we don't have any minutes or any notes for meetings on the 9th of April or the 10th of April. Now, I will tell you in fairness to you, we do have minutes of a VJ collegium meeting on the 9th of April, which apparently took place at the VMA, the Military Medical Academy. Do you recall whether or not there were any evening briefings on April 9th or April 10th of 1999; and if so, whether any notes were taken?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right now I can't remember every single day of those 50 days. I did say that in principle this was an order, and indeed there were briefings every evening. Perhaps the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, General Ojdanic, was not there for each of these briefings, but I believe his attendance rate was over 98 per cent. Someone else might have been there for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But on those rare occasions when he wasn't in attendance, someone else presided and notes were taken, correct?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And let me show you one more I think. It's -- this would be e-court 110 -- I'm sorry, my numbering is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we go back one more page to 109.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is the last page from the notes of the meeting of the 15th of April. I have an English translation of this meeting but not the last thing at the bottom where I read: "Belgrade, 15 April 1999." Can you tell me what's written or printed above that? It's just looks like an acronym or abbreviations. SVK, is that the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Supreme Command Staff, Belgrade, 15th of April, 1999. The handwriting belongs to Colonel Paskas. It was this collegium meeting that the deputy Chief of the General Staff chaired because it reflects clearly that the final contribution was made by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I have a question about the use of terms regarding who attended the evening meetings. Because we've heard reference to the VJ collegium and we've heard reference to during the wartime the staff of the Supreme Command. Now, what -- what group was it that met in the evenings for the briefings? Was that the collegium? Was that just generals and colonels who needed to know about what was going on? What was the name of this group that met for the evening briefings or did you have a name?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told attorney Visnjic yesterday that this was a briefing which has its place, role, and importance in the work of commands in combat operations. Based on orders, briefings were to be attended by those directly subordinated, these being deputy Chief of the General Staff, sector chiefs, and chiefs of independent administrations, the security administration and the morale and information administration. In the operations staff centre there was the operations administration and the information administration. So these were the bodies that made up the leading segments of the command post. They attended briefings every day. They made proposals and they briefed the chief of the Supreme Command Staff on certain decisions, and then he transformed these into tasks and assignments. For the most part this was sectorial work. Each person briefed the chief on their own work, on their own jobs, and they would make proposals for decisions. Sometimes the chief would put together teams to deal with operative and strategic problems. These briefings were attended by what we in the army call a number of officers below the line who had no right to take any decisions; rather, as I said yesterday, they carried out preparations and created conditions for these briefings to take place. They would take minutes, they would make sure all the conditions were in place and all the appropriate documents were kept. These were normally chiefs or shift leaders in the operations sector. I led one of these shifts and the other was led by Colonel Paskas. As you have seen, by the 5th of April there had been other people involved keeping minutes, but after the 5th of April it boiled down to the two of us alone. As for those below the line who attended these briefings, there was the chef de cabinet precisely because of setting up these -- creating these assignments, that the Chief of Staff the Supreme Command later signed and that were later submitted to all these subordinate units. So that was his job.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the make-up of the General Staff of the army prior to the onset of the war? Do you know who the -- you don't have to name them for me but I've seen minutes of those meetings and it looks like there was in the neighbourhood of 15, less than 20 of generals who attended the meetings of the collegium; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we'd have to do some calculations, but if you want me to I can rely on my memory to name all the generals for you and I think I might get over 90 per cent of them right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If that won't take you more than a couple minutes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it won't. Meetings were regularly attended by deputy Chief of the General Staff or Chief of the General Staff or the Supreme Command Staff, Lieutenant-General -- Colonel-General Dragoljub Ojdanic; also his deputy, Colonel-General Svetozar Marjanovic. Sector chiefs, the operations staff sector Lieutenant-General Obradovic later moved to a different post and was replaced by Lieutenant-General Blagoje Kovacevic. Sector chiefs for the various branches and arms of service, at first it was General Panic and then General Simic for the land forces. For the air force and air defence at the outset there was Grahovac and then was followed by General Velickovic, who was tragically killed at a combat position and then was followed by Karanovic. For the navy, Admiral Novkovic [as interpreted]. For recruitment and mobilisation, Lieutenant-General Ratomir who later moved to a different position and was replaced by General Matovic. For signals, IT, and electronic activity, Lieutenant-Colonel Andjelkovic. Sector chief for logistics, Lieutenant-General Pantelic. Chief of the information administration, General Branko Krga. Chief of the information administration, General -- intelligence administration Curcin Djordje, General Geza Farkas, and sometimes also General Gajic who would stand in for him. And on behalf of the morale administration --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there because the two minutes are up but you've done very well. This group during the wartime as I understand it then became the Supreme Command Staff; is that correct? Or was that made up of different personnel?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Supreme Command Staff is an organ of the supreme commander, which prepares, organizes, and secures implementation and control of orders in a wartime situation. By definition, this is the General Staff, but the scope of the General Staff is comprehensively reduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And the Supreme Command Staff you say was I guess an organ of the supreme commander which we know was Slobodan Milosevic. Was there in addition to him a body that was called the Supreme Command? He's the supreme commander, but was there a body composed of him and other individuals that was sometimes referred to as the Supreme Command during the war, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know. This is a little difficult to explain to nonprofessionals, but I'll try to explain briefly as follows. The Supreme Command comprises the supreme commander and the Supreme Command Staff. The supreme commander under the constitution of the FRY published in Official Gazette number 1 dated the 27th of April, 1992, Article 135 reads --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You don't have to --

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- That the president of the republic --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We've got that in evidence. We know about that. But my question is: In addition to the supreme commander and the Supreme Command Staff that you told us about, was there anyone else who was part of the Supreme Command or is it your position that the Supreme Command was only Mr. Milosevic and those members of the General Staff who became part of the Supreme Command Staff during the war? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, you interrupted me, and that's why I couldn't tell you. Article -- paragraph 2 of Article 135 says that the president of the republic commands the army, in keeping with any decisions made by the Supreme Defence Council. The Supreme Defence Council in addition to the president of the republic, president of the FRY, also includes the presidents of all member republics. Therefore, the Supreme Defence Council as a whole under the constitution and according to our theory was incorporated and was part of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when we requested documents from Serbia about meetings of the Supreme Defence Council during the war, the response -- the official response we got was that there were no meetings of the Supreme Defence Council during the war. Yet it seems hard to imagine how the president and the supreme commander, Mr. Milosevic, during a state of war if he's supposed to command the army in conjunction with decisions of the Supreme Defence Council could have done that without them meeting. So do you know how that happened, because obviously the army was being commanded during the war?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was ex officio that I only had contacts with the operations department and the VJ. As for the president and the Supreme Defence Council, I was not in touch with them and I can't tell you anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Milosevic around the building during the war?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see him once at the beginning of the war when he came to the operations centre or room, and twice when he came back in the evening to rest with his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. What about Mr. Milutinovic, did you ever see him during the war?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I also saw him several times also when he came. We would meet in passing when he came in the evening there to rest with his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And President Djukanovic?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw President Djukanovic during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions for the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do have a couple of questions. I'll be relatively brief. Can we please have 3D1085. This is about a conclusion made by the Government of Serbia and can we please have page 8 in the B/C/S and page 5 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, General. We shall not be reading this. The Judges can see it for themselves. My question: Mr. Hannis asked you about certain blanks or voids in the body of the text, and you provided some answers. My question: What you told Mr. Hannis is that consistent with the explanation--

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have an objection concerning this document. It was not listed as one of the documents to be used with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that's quite correct, but I'm using this to further elucidate something that Mr. Hannis raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't have any objection to the contents of this because they clear up some of the questions I have, but I have an objection about the way this was done. Because if I had had this and known it was going to be used with this witness, I wouldn't have been asking questions about why that page is missing in the other notes because I know from reading this. So it looks like I was ambushed and that's my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you have to say about that, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I mentioned this document twice in the courtroom when I provided some explanations about Exhibit 84, I think that was the abridged version of the briefing. Mr. Hannis has been aware of this document. I didn't want to raise this with this witness. I thought that the document that was disclosed to Mr. Hannis spoke for itself. This is not ambush. We explained through this document why the previous version is incorrect, why it -- why some pages were missing. I know that he didn't know that I would be using this document with this witness, but it was not my intention to do it. I assumed that Mr. Hannis would be able to see from the document what this is all about. After all, the document speaks for itself. That is true. But I simply didn't want to leave some things unresolved before we continue with the trial. I'm sorry, the document was 1087, that was the document that we received from the Serbian government with just half of the pages that we wanted to use. So it's 3D1088.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You started at 3D1085. What is the document we're using?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we're using 3D1085, that's the conclusion of the Serbian government that we received together with the document 3D1088. The document 3D1088 should be the same as the document that we were talking about today, that's 3D1094, but unfortunately it contains just half of the pages. It's a little bit complicated, but that's how it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The suggestion, Mr. Hannis, is that the document's been disclosed. I know it's one of thousands disclosed, but that its number is so close to this as to make it something that you should have realised assisted in interpreting 3D1008 -- sorry, 1088.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I wouldn't have spent five or ten minutes of my limited cross-examination time asking about missing pages when the answer is in this document. I would have appreciated the courtesy of an interruption at that time saying Mr. Hannis doesn't need to do that, that's in this document. That's the essence of my objection. I appreciate the content, but still it doesn't explain the absence of any notes for the meeting on the 19th of April if I read it correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What we'll do is allow you to ask the question you wish to ask, Mr. Visnjic, in spite of not including this document on your list; and in the overall time-keeping exercise, we'll have with regard to the fact that the cross-examination would not have exceeded your examination-in-chief but for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you've looked at the document. Could you comment on the explanation provided here by the Serbian government?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can comment on it. I think that this is -- because this is signed by the secretary of Ministry of Defence that this was a serious work and there is no reason to suspect anything here. I can't tell you anything more about it because I didn't do anything about it, I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Does this description in the last few lines correspond to what you knew and what you actually did during the war?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that if the -- everything that is in handwriting, all the manuscript, if this is copied then nothing was lost because I said those conclusions were just more orderly version of the conclusions made by the chief of the Supreme Command Staff at the end. They were typed up. Afterwards he went through them and he checked every word. So we really had to have it for the sake of accuracy, but no substantial changes had been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move on, I'm not following this. The sections were removed for photocopying purposes and then restored. Why weren't they also photocopied? Does it say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here that it's not photocopied, but if I were to show a document -- one of these documents to the witness, perhaps he will then have a better idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All -- this is meaningless evidence so far, Mr. Visnjic, it's not conveying anything to me about what the witness knows about what happened. He doesn't plainly know what has happened indeed the ministry in producing this copy for you. So what is it you think he can help us with when the letter itself doesn't actually solve the mystery entirely?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I understood it - and I don't know whether I should be going into this in front of the witness - but it is obvious that in addition to this notebook or in this notebook some documents were pasted in. They are not part of the manuscript, what is handwritten in the notebook, and those documents were then removed. This is what the witness told Mr. Hannis in response to one of his questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that doesn't make it all right, Mr. Visnjic; that just raises suspicion. And there isn't a solution to any suspicion that there might be. It seems very strange when the bits removed could easily be copied and returned to you to complete the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. The parts that were removed -- I can only assume why this was done. The parts that were removed were other documents that were pasted into the notebook. So you have the handwritten notebook and the documents that are inserted in this notebook. So when I submitted my request to the government, I asked for the notebook. The fact that they decided not to give me the whole notebook, or rather, not to give me both the documents and the notebook, that was up to the government, it was -- I had nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm suggesting that you should go back to the government and get the rest of it and give us the whole picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I -- I have already done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good. Well, let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I just wanted to show you a sample document that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D493, or rather, 3D487, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, are you familiar with this document or such documents?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you can see here in the heading, you see the cabinet of the Chief of Staff. Let me just see, the date is the 8th of June -- yes, yes, I'm familiar with this document because I was at the command post at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And what is this document?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is what we were talking about a little while ago. After the briefing was over, the chef de cabinet, together with us from the operations administration --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on a minute, Mr. Mucibabic. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think this is another document that was not listed as going to be used with this witness and I'm not sure how it arises from cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Hannis asked the witness why there were those blanks in the document. The witness replied that he assumed that the blanks were the consequence of some documents that had been pasted into the notebook being removed. Now, in order to clear this up I'm showing the witness one of such documents that have already been used as exhibits in this trial and the witness has just identified it. Nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It should be foreseeable, though, that you would be using these documents, Mr. Visnjic, and they should have been on the list intimating what you were likely to be referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is the only document that's on my list right from the start because that was the only document that I had. In light of the problems with the briefing notebook that I got from the government - and believe me, I've been trying to get it for three years and I could not know what they would send me, whether they would send me the whole thing or whether some parts would be taken out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think you're being fair, Mr. Visnjic. At the end of last week you produced intimation of the material that you would use with this witness, and this exhibit and the previous one were not on it. And you must have foreseen the distinct possibility of using these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, quite frankly, I didn't know what direction the cross-examination by the Prosecution would take --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's pretty obvious if you have a book with gaps in it that the cross-examination is going to wonder -- look for an explanation for the gaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, yes. I do accept that this is a mistake on my part, but the only reason why I'm doing this is to clear this up, nothing else. We will do everything we can to obtain the complete document and to supply it to the Trial Chamber if, in no other way, then as a bar table exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there anything else you want to ask about this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mucibabic, was it the practice for you or your colleagues to put into the book in which you were recording what happened at the meeting other documents, apart from conclusions that you've already told us about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I think that attorney Visnjic, by showing this document, in fact confirmed what I said. All those tasks are listed in the handwritten minutes, but not -- they are not as accurately as defined, you don't have the deadline, you don't have the person responsible, and cooperation. In order to be able to follow things and to have everything in one place, we pasted it in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. My question is rather different. I want to know if there were any other documents, perhaps associated with the meeting or perhaps associated with matters which arose at the meeting, which you would also paste into the notebook.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While I was in charge of the minute-taking, no. That was the only thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Anything further, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no, nothing related to this witness, but I would just like to notify you that one of the missing minutes on the 19th of April we disclosed it to the Prosecution as 3D590 in the printed version, not in the handwritten version, and 3D724, the minutes of the 6th of April we -- it was also disclosed to the Prosecution. So this is not for re-examination. This is just -- we're just giving notice to the Prosecution so that they can find their way around the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I imagine that 3D590 has further raised the hackles of Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It has, Your Honour. I have that, so it appears that original notes of that must have existed some place else other than within this document which purports to be the entire document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So where did that come? Why is it not in the book? Your Honour, my concern about these evening briefing notes goes back to the Prosecution case. One of these pages was introduced during the Prosecution case, and I raised a concern at the time because what we had was a typewritten Cyrillic with no stamp, no date, et cetera, then we had this explanation, but I had a concern about it. Now as I understand the explanation now is at the end of the meeting this witness or the note-taker would meet with someone to discuss the taskings and the conclusions that were reached and then they were reformulated and typed up. Well, that -- I consider that a part of that entire document. We should have that, because it may turn out that this guy, this general, is the good note-taker and his notes are almost identical to the final formulation, but Colonel Paskas, he may be terrible, and if he's terrible with regard to the conclusions and the taskings, then other things in the notes he takes for the day there could be a question about too. So we should have that entire thing to have a fair evaluation of what it is. I'm in a bit of a dilemma because I like lots of things that are in these notes, but I don't feel comfortable because we have an incomplete picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think Mr. Visnjic recognises that and is endeavouring to complete the picture and will note what you've said that the provision of a typewritten copy of what has originally been handwritten is rather different from the typewritten copies of the nature the witness is telling us been added into the book. So the 19th of April still presents a problem for us if you do not have the handwritten version.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we don't have it either. It's obvious that those things are missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, good hunting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, that brings your evidence to an end. Thank you for coming here to give us evidence. You're now free to leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Good-bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good timing, Mr. Visnjic. We can break now and resume at five past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, you wish to raise something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I wanted to raise an objection as to the next witness. It's the Prosecution's position that his evidence is not relevant to any pertinent issue in the case. If the Court disagrees with me, however, I do have an objection about it his 92 ter statement. In a more particularised fashion, I object in particular to paragraphs 11 through 14 and 16 to 19, talking in some details about depleted uranium and the effects on human life, et cetera. I think the witness is purporting to testify as an expert in that regard, Your Honour, and the expert witness procedures haven't been complied with in connection with him. Paragraph 15 I think is not relevant. It talks about bombing certain facilities within Serbia proper, not in Kosovo, and if those -- if those paragraphs were not taken into evidence, I would not object to the rest of his 92 ter statement and might have just a handful of questions about I think paragraphs 6 and 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm trying to distribute what Mr. Hannis said -- I'm actually going to begin with the main objection. Our intention is via this witnesses to indicate to the Court the intensity and the seriousness of the NATO attacks and the fact that nothing stopped them from carrying out their ultimate objective or their ultimate plan in relation to the entry of their troops into the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Other than that, this witness is going to testify about the preparations of the Army of Yugoslavia, beginning from the start of the year, for the defence of the country which I think could be something that can relate to the part that concerns planning. Then in relation to the locations where specific weapons, specific types of weapons were used, we believe that the testimony of this witness also indicates the seriousness of the possibility of a land operation or indicates what General Ojdanic and his team believed when they were preparing for the defence of the country from the NATO attack. And of course ultimately the testimony of this witness concerns also the effect of the intensity and the manner of the bombing and the use of the weapons on the civilian population and possibly their movements in the course of combat. [In English] Your Honour, I think Mr. Sepenuk wishes to add something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in the transcript here Mr. Visnjic said - and this is on line 14, 15, our intention is via this witness to indicate to the Court the intensity and the seriousness of the NATO attacks and the fact that nothing stopped them from carrying out their ultimate objective, I think what Mr. Visnjic said, at least what I thought he said was NATO would stop at nothing from carrying out their ultimate objective, i.e., including the use of depleted uranium and cluster bombs, not nothing stopped them from carrying out, but NATO would stop at nothing for carrying out their ultimate objective. And I don't know how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, what is the source of the information at the beginning of paragraph 11 and at the beginning of paragraph 20?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that this is something that we need to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you should know that, Mr. Visnjic. Tell me what the source is as far as you're aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the Army of Yugoslavia made certain assessments in terms of weapons and the quantity. I'm looking at what was in question the enriched uranium projectiles and what was used by NATO, or rather, that during the war they marked and indicated the places where the weapons were used.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It was depleted uranium projectiles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, looking at the paragraphs that the particular challenge is made to, was this witness involved in actually analysing any of the samples of contaminated material?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this witness was the chief of the service that was carrying out those assignments. I don't know if he personally went, but in any case he was at the head of the service that was doing this job and whose task it was. And you will see from the witness that it was him who actually issued some orders in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And paragraph 15, is any of the locations in paragraph 15 in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes, but the others are not?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The others are not. Actually, this is a specific consequence of the bombing here relating to industrial facilities, and in this case industrial facilities in Pristina were most probably targeted which caused a specific type of pollution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, the highest we think it can be stated is that much of this evidence is of doubtful relevancy rather than clearly irrelevant, and being charged with the responsibility of viewing the whole picture so far as it is at all relevant to the issues in the case, then we think that we should hear the evidence of this witness. And because there are specific areas where you would be taking objection if we did not do this, we shall reserve the question of the relevancy of this evidence until we have heard it and perhaps even longer than that. It may be we can deal with it as soon as we've heard it or in the final deliberations. But let's look at that once we've heard what the witness has to say. Mr. Visnjic, his name?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our witness is General Slobodan Petkovic. He's going to testify under 92 ter, viva voce, and the statement is 3D1119, that is his -- the exhibit that is his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document being shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll now be examined by Mr. Visnjic on behalf of Mr. Ojdanic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, good day.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, can you please tell us what your duties were in 1999?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1999 I was the chief of the atomic, biological, and chemical defence administration of the Army of Yugoslavia. When the -- when the bombing began of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, I was at the staff of the Supreme Command performing the function of the chief of the nuclear, biological, chemical, and defence branch in the land army service.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, the first time was when you met -- or when you encountered the -- when did you first encounter the possibility of depleted uranium ammunition being used?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: The first time that type of ammunition was used or an indication of that was in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When you felt that this ammunition could be used in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Our estimates actually led us to believe --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, when? Can you please tell me the time-frame?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: This was in early 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at Exhibit 3D -- [In English] Your Honour, I'm sorry. [Interpretation] It's Friday, so we're rushing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, I would like to ask you something before that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: On the 23rd of August, 2007, you talked to investigators from the Defence team of General Ojdanic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When you arrived at The Hague did you sign a statement that was prepared then as a draft?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Would you, if you were to testify, give the same answers now as you gave then?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would, I would answer in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we please look at Exhibit 3D1119.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at Defence Exhibit 3D1099 in the e-court and can we please look at page 2 in the B/C/S and page 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, can you please look at the document in front of you. It's dated the 12th of February, 1999. Can you please tell me what kind of a document this is.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: This is an instruction we sent to the 3rd Army command in view of information that the NATO forces used weapons with higher radiation. We informed them about the characteristics of these weapons and measures that should be undertaken in the event that these projectiles were used in a possible attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't want to look through the whole document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 4, please, of the document in B/C/S and page 5 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Can you please look at the conclusion part of the document, item 1.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what this means: "Given the conduct of the NATO alliance in international relations, the opinions expressed by the international community ..." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: When I said that in this document, what I meant was this: Having the experience and knowing what the situation in international relations was and the conduct of similar forces during the aggression on Iraq and similar situations and that the international community did not condemn such a thing, I expected since we have the information that they did have this sort of weapons and ammunition at their disposal and it was to be expected that these arms would be used if the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were to be bombed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please now look at paragraph 10 of the conclusion, it's on the same page, and in the English text it's on page 6. Thank you. From what I can see, certain measures are planned here. Can you please explain more in detail this third measure where it says: "In sectors where high radiation is detected," and what does this ZS, "Ziva Sila," mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: It just means humans, cattle, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what you ordered the units to do in relation to this item in this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: There is a protocol of how to act in situations when nuclear chemical or weapons with a higher degree of radiation are used. Units reconnoitre with the appropriate means, and if there are any doubts or if there is evidence that there is a nuclear or chemical danger to the population and the area, then the boundaries of the contaminated area are established, signs are posted, warning signs, which is in accordance to regulations, and all movement and staying in the area by the population or soldiers is forbidden in that area until decontamination is completed or if there is evidence that there is no more contamination in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now in that same paragraph we have something that reads: "The missile is to be removed in the presence of the 'verifiers,' and this if possible should be filmed." What verifiers are we looking at here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind what was going on in Kosovo and bearing in mind what was going on with all the units and measures that were being taken, everything that we were doing without this being verified by the verifiers was not recognised -- being recognised by the international community. It was very difficult to predict what would happen in the territory; and having said that, I believed that it was necessary for the verification teams who were in the area at the time when I wrote this should continue in the eventuality of air-strikes to try to prove this so that we received confirmation from them. They were representatives of the international community, after all, and they had to see this as far as we were concerned so that we had hard evidence of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The last paragraph envisages a special place for this toxic material to be dumped, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: This was dangerous, radioactive waste, potentially dangerous for animal and human life as well as vegetal life. It was our responsibility to pick it up and leave it in special containers in certain special places that were free of human presence in order to prevent any form of contamination. These dumping locations were permanent or provisional radiotoxic waste--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Move to something relevant. What happened after these weapons were dropped is irrelevant to the issues in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, let us move now to the same document, 3D1099, page 1 of that document. General, what is about to turn up on the screen in front of you is a document dated the 5th of March, 1999, this is about three weeks before the outbreak of war. Can you please tell us what is being requested in this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Given the fact that we believed and in fact had information indicating that NATO had ammunition containing depleted uranium in their possession, different calibres and varying amounts, we asked the information administration of the General Staff of the VJ, which was the service in charge of collecting intelligence, to put together for our purposes information on the deployment of forces in the surrounding area and on the type and nature of the ammunition that was available to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And then the next sentence reads: "As we speak, NATO troops are being deployed in Macedonia."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: We had information indicating that NATO units were deploying in the Republic of Macedonia. We assumed that some of those units might, in fact, have this type of ammunition available to them and we requested information and intelligence so that we might be able to put in a timely reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, as far as I can see by looking at this table, we're not talking about missiles and ammunition used by aeroplanes. There are other types of ammunition involved. Can you tell us more about that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just stop there for the moment. What we would like to know, Mr. Visnjic, is the information you actually got, not what you were seeking. What's the relevance of writing letters indicating a suspicion of the existence of such material. Let's hear what actually was discovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we'll move on to our next document. 3D1100.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, when you received intelligence about this exhibit, did you do anything about it? Did you perform any activities about this? What activities? And what is this document about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just add to what the Presiding Judge asked of you a while ago. We received confirmation that this type of ammunition and these amounts were available to them. They had 20-millimetre guns; two 30-millimetre guns; and howitzers, 155-millimetre. In answer to your question before we -- we took measures --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second. Is what you've just said referring to events in Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in Macedonia. I was talking about the NATO forces who at this point in time had this or that type of ammunition available to them and they were stationed at Petrovac airport.
